name: Ectopic pregnancy
subtitle: Diagnosis and medical or surgical management
oneLine: Extrauterine blastocyst implantation, early diagnostic triaging, and medical or surgical intervention

emphasis.skill.particulars.demographics: Age in the reproductive years, parity, and calculated gestational age from the last menstrual period set the pre-test probability of early pregnancy complications.

emphasis.skill.hx.chief_complaints: In early pregnancy, unilateral pelvic pain, abnormal vaginal bleeding, and amenorrhoea form the classic triad, but atypical presentations with fainting, diarrhea, or shoulder tip pain must never be overlooked.
emphasis.skill.hx.obg.booking_lmp: Accurate dating from the last menstrual period calculates the expected gestational age and determines whether an intrauterine gestational sac should be visible on transvaginal ultrasonography.
emphasis.skill.hx.obg.gynae_symptoms: Unilateral pelvic pain starting as a dull ache and becoming sharp or colicky is the hallmark of tubal distension, while shoulder-tip pain signifies diaphragmatic irritation from internal haemorrhage.
emphasis.skill.hx.obg.menstrual_history: Characteristically, vaginal bleeding in ectopic pregnancy is dark brown and scanty, representing endometrial decidual breakdown rather than heavy active arterial flow with clots.

chapters.title: Past, personal, drug and family history

emphasis.skill.hx.obg.previous_pregnancies: A previous ectopic pregnancy is the single strongest clinical risk factor, carrying a ten-fold increase in recurrence.
emphasis.skill.hx.obg.gynae_background: Enquire specifically about past pelvic inflammatory disease, tubal surgery, sterilisation reversal, and contraception failure with an intrauterine contraceptive device.

emphasis.skill.gen.appearance: Look for pallor, cold clammy extremities, and distress indicating internal haemorrhage before abdominal palpation begins.
emphasis.skill.gen.vitals: Tachycardia above 100 beats per minute and postural hypotension or blood pressure below 100/60 mmHg indicate ruptured ectopic pregnancy with hemoperitoneum.

emphasis.skill.exam.obg.gynae_abdominal: Localised tenderness in the iliac fossa with voluntary guarding indicates tubal inflammation; generalised peritonism with rebound tenderness signals substantial haemoperitoneum.
emphasis.skill.exam.obg.bimanual: Cervical motion tenderness (excitation) and an exquisite adnexal mass separate from the uterus are cardinal signs; palpate very gently to avoid provoking tubal rupture.

skill.ectopic.basics.title: Implantation sites and mechanisms of tubal damage
skill.ectopic.basics.oneLine: Where blastocysts lodge outside the cavity, and why the tube ruptures
skill.ectopic.basics.why: Understanding the anatomical sites of ectopic implantation explains why presentations differ: an ampullary pregnancy aborts into the peritoneum with subtle symptoms, an isthmic pregnancy ruptures early, and a cornual pregnancy ruptures late with catastrophic bleeding.

teach.heading: Anatomical sites of extrauterine implantation
teach.body:
More than ninety-five percent of ectopic pregnancies lodge within the fallopian tube. The ampulla is the most common site, accommodating approximately seventy percent of tubal gestations due to its wide lumen.

The isthmus accounts for twelve percent; its narrow and non-distensible lumen leads to early rupture between six and eight weeks of gestation. The fimbrial end accounts for eleven percent, often terminating in tubal abortion.

Interstitial or cornual implantations represent two to three percent. Because the surrounding myometrium provides initial distension, rupture occurs later, between twelve and sixteen weeks, resulting in catastrophic haemorrhage from uterine artery branches.

Non-tubal gestations are rare, comprising ovarian (three percent), caesarean scar (one percent), cervical (under one percent), and abdominal pregnancies.

teach.heading: Pathophysiology: erosion, rupture, and tubal abortion
teach.body:
Unlike the uterus, the fallopian tube possesses no submucosa and forms little or no decidual barrier. The trophoblast invades directly into the muscular wall and penetrates blood vessels.

As the conceptus grows, blood collects within the lumen, producing haematosalpinx. Progressive distension stretches the tubal serosa, causing sharp pelvic pain.

If the gestational sac separates from the tubal wall near the fimbria, it is extruded into the peritoneal cavity as a tubal abortion, often accompanied by recurrent low-grade intra-abdominal bleeding.

If invasion erodes the tubal wall, rupture occurs. Arterial bleeding into the peritoneal cavity produces haemoperitoneum, subdiaphragmatic irritation, and hypovolaemic shock.

probes.q: Which part of the fallopian tube is the most frequent site of ectopic implantation?
probes.a: The ampulla is the most frequent site of tubal ectopic implantation, accounting for approximately seventy percent of cases.

probes.q: Why does an interstitial or cornual ectopic pregnancy rupture later than an isthmic pregnancy?
probes.a: The interstitial portion of the tube is surrounded by thick myometrium that accommodates greater growth before rupturing at twelve to sixteen weeks.

probes.q: Why does trophoblast invasion into the fallopian tube cause rapid tissue destruction compared to intrauterine implantation?
probes.a: The fallopian tube lacks a protective submucosa and well-developed decidual layer, allowing trophoblastic cells to invade directly into the muscularis and blood vessels.

rubric.text: Identifies the relative frequencies of ampullary, isthmic, fimbrial and cornual ectopic pregnancies
Correlates tubal anatomy with the timing and severity of rupture
Explains how the absence of a decidual barrier facilitates tubal invasion and bleeding

skill.ectopic.signs.title: Clinical presentation: the classic triad, atypical masquerades, and signs of rupture
skill.ectopic.signs.oneLine: Recognising pelvic pain, spotting, cervical motion tenderness, and haemoperitoneum
skill.ectopic.signs.why: Over half of ectopic pregnancies present without the textbook triad. Recognising cervical motion tenderness, adnexal fullness, and referred shoulder tip pain saves lives before overt haemorrhagic shock supervenes.

teach.heading: The clinical presentation and cardinal symptoms
teach.body:
The textbook triad consists of amenorrhoea, unilateral lower abdominal pain, and abnormal vaginal bleeding. However, fewer than fifty percent of women exhibit all three features together.

Amenorrhoea of six to eight weeks is usual, but fifteen to twenty percent of women experience spotting around their expected period and report no missed menses.

Pain is the most consistent symptom. It typically begins as a dull, unilateral ache in the iliac fossa and progresses to sharp, colicky spasms as the tube distends.

Vaginal bleeding is characteristically dark brown and scanty, with a prune-juice appearance, resulting from endometrial decidual sloughing rather than active bleeding from the tube. Occasionally an intact decidual cast is expelled.

teach.heading: Physical examination and signs of internal haemorrhage
teach.body:
Abdominal examination reveals localised tenderness and voluntary guarding in the affected iliac fossa. Generalised peritonism with rebound tenderness suggests significant haemoperitoneum.

On pelvic examination, cervical motion tenderness (excitation or the Chandelier sign) is elicited by moving the cervix; stretching the pelvic peritoneum overlying the inflamed tube produces acute pain.

A tender, boggy adnexal mass separate from the uterus is palpable in approximately half of patients. Gentle palpation is critical to prevent iatrogenic rupture.

Diaphragmatic irritation from haemoperitoneum causes referred shoulder-tip pain. Blood pooling in the pouch of Douglas causes rectal pressure and tenesmus. Tachycardia above one hundred beats per minute and hypotension signify severe rupture.

probes.q: What is the characteristic colour and origin of vaginal bleeding in ectopic pregnancy?
probes.a: The bleeding is characteristically dark brown and scanty, arising from endometrial decidual sloughing caused by falling hormonal support.

probes.q: What is the clinical significance of referred shoulder tip pain in a woman with suspected ectopic pregnancy?
probes.a: Referred shoulder tip pain indicates haemoperitoneum irritating the phrenic nerve endings on the undersurface of the diaphragm.

probes.q: What is cervical motion tenderness and how does it arise in tubal pregnancy?
probes.a: Cervical motion tenderness is severe pain produced by gentle cervical displacement, which stretches the inflamed pelvic peritoneum adjacent to the affected fallopian tube.

rubric.text: Lists the classical triad and notes that fewer than half of women present with all three
Describes the dark brown scanty nature of decidual sloughing bleeding
Identifies cervical motion tenderness and its peritoneal basis
Recognises shoulder tip pain and tenesmus as warning signs of internal haemorrhage

skill.ectopic.summary.title: Clinical summary in suspected ectopic pregnancy
skill.ectopic.summary.oneLine: Synthesising the clinical picture, haemodynamic state, and risk profile
skill.ectopic.summary.why: A concise summary in early pregnancy pain immediately separates the stable patient who can undergo transvaginal ultrasound from the woman in impending haemorrhagic shock who needs simultaneous resuscitation and theatre transfer.

teach.heading: Synthesising the clinical summary
teach.body:
A structured summary synthesises six core elements: age and parity; calculated gestational age from the last menstrual period; presence of the classic triad; haemodynamic stability; localised or generalised peritoneal signs; and key predisposing risk factors.

Classifying the patient as haemodynamically stable versus unstable is the single most vital operational distinction.

In a stable patient, the summary directs immediate transvaginal ultrasound and quantitative serum beta-hCG testing.

In an unstable patient, the summary establishes immediate transfer to the operating theatre with concurrent intravenous volume and blood resuscitation.

rows: Urgent transvaginal scan and baseline beta-hCG
Positive test, no pain, empty uterus

probes.q: What is the primary objective of the clinical summary in early pregnancy acute abdomen?
probes.a: To determine immediate haemodynamic stability and differentiate patients requiring emergency resuscitation from those safe for diagnostic imaging.

probes.q: What clinical features place a patient in the unstable or ruptured ectopic category?
probes.a: Tachycardia, hypotension, syncope, pallor, generalised peritonism, and shoulder tip pain indicative of massive internal haemorrhage.

rubric.text: Includes gestation, clinical triad, haemodynamic vitals, and peritoneal signs in the summary

skill.ectopic.differential.title: Differential diagnosis of first-trimester pelvic pain and bleeding
skill.ectopic.differential.oneLine: Distinguishing ectopic pregnancy from miscarriage, ovarian accidents, and acute appendicitis
skill.ectopic.differential.why: Miscarriage, ruptured corpus luteum, ovarian torsion, pelvic infection, and appendicitis all present with pelvic pain and a missed period or irregular bleeding. Distinguishing them requires correlating ultrasound morphology with the hCG level and systemic signs.

teach.heading: Obstetric and early pregnancy look-alikes
teach.body:
Threatened miscarriage presents with vaginal bleeding and central cramping suprapubic pain. On ultrasound, a viable intrauterine pregnancy with a cardiac flicker is seen, and the internal cervical os remains closed.

Incomplete miscarriage presents with heavy vaginal bleeding and passing of clots or tissue through an open cervical os. Ultrasound shows retained products within a distended uterine cavity.

A ruptured corpus luteal cyst occurs in early pregnancy and causes sudden unilateral pelvic pain with a positive pregnancy test. On ultrasound, an intrauterine sac is visible, and the ovary displays a thick-walled vascular cyst (the ring of fire) with fluid in the cul-de-sac.

Heterotopic pregnancy must be considered in women undergoing assisted reproductive technology.

rows: Adnexal mass separate from ovary, empty uterus
Central cramping, bright bleeding, closed os
Intrauterine gestational sac with fetal cardiac flicker
Sudden sharp pain after intercourse or exercise
Intrauterine pregnancy present, cystic ovarian mass
Periumbilical pain migrating to right iliac fossa

probes.q: How does the pain of threatened miscarriage differ in location and nature from tubal ectopic pregnancy?
probes.a: Threatened miscarriage pain is central, suprapubic, and cramping, whereas ectopic pregnancy pain is classically unilateral, lateralised to one iliac fossa, and sharp or colicky.

probes.q: What ultrasound finding distinguishes a ruptured corpus luteal cyst from an ectopic pregnancy?
probes.a: A ruptured corpus luteum cyst is located within the ovary and is typically accompanied by a normal intrauterine gestational sac, whereas an ectopic pregnancy is seen in the adnexa separate from the ovary with an empty uterus.

skill.ix.ectopic.workup.title: Diagnostic workup: transvaginal ultrasound, serial beta-hCG, and discriminatory zone
skill.ix.ectopic.workup.oneLine: Correlating imaging features with serial biochemical markers to locate the pregnancy
skill.ix.ectopic.workup.why: A single beta-hCG value never locates a pregnancy. Combining high-resolution transvaginal ultrasound with serial 48-hour beta-hCG curves identifies tubal ectopics before rupture and guides non-surgical options.

teach.heading: Transvaginal ultrasound landmarks and signs
teach.body:
Transvaginal ultrasound is the primary diagnostic modality, achieving sensitivity exceeding ninety percent. Examination must evaluate both adnexa, the uterine cavity, and the pouch of Douglas.

Definitive confirmation is the visualisation of an extrauterine gestational sac containing a yolk sac or embryo with cardiac activity, separate from the ovary.

The tubal ring or bagel sign is a concentric, brightly hyperechoic ring surrounding a small gestational sac within the fallopian tube.

An inhomogeneous or complex adnexal mass (the blob sign) is the most common sonographic appearance, representing haemorrhage and trophoblast within the tube.

Uterine signs include an empty cavity or a pseudogestational sac, which is a centrally located fluid collection lacking the double decidual sign of true intrauterine pregnancy. Echogenic fluid in the pouch of Douglas confirms haemoperitoneum.

teach.heading: Serial serum beta-hCG and the discriminatory zone
teach.body:
In a viable intrauterine pregnancy, serum beta-hCG rises by more than sixty-three percent every forty-eight hours. An abnormal rise of less than sixty-three percent or a plateau indicates a non-viable pregnancy or ectopic gestation.

The discriminatory zone is the serum beta-hCG threshold above which an intrauterine gestational sac should always be visible on transvaginal ultrasound, typically between fifteen hundred and two thousand international units per litre.

If the beta-hCG is above the discriminatory zone and the uterine cavity is empty, ectopic pregnancy is presumed until proven otherwise.

A pregnancy of unknown location (PUL) is diagnosed when the pregnancy test is positive but transvaginal scan demonstrates neither an intrauterine nor an extrauterine gestation. Serum beta-hCG must be repeated forty-eight hours later to calculate the percentage change.

probes.q: What is the transvaginal ultrasound discriminatory zone for serum beta-hCG?
probes.a: The discriminatory zone is fifteen hundred to two thousand international units per litre, above which an intrauterine gestational sac should always be visible on transvaginal scan.

probes.q: What sonographic features differentiate a pseudogestational sac from a true early intrauterine pregnancy?
probes.a: A pseudogestational sac is a central fluid collection without a double decidual sign or yolk sac, whereas a true early intrauterine sac is eccentric and displays a double decidual ring.

probes.q: How is a pregnancy of unknown location managed when initial transvaginal ultrasound is inconclusive?
probes.a: Serum beta-hCG is measured at baseline and repeated forty-eight hours later to determine the trajectory: a rise above sixty-three percent suggests intrauterine pregnancy, a fall above fifty percent suggests failing pregnancy, and a plateau warrants early review for ectopic.

skill.ectopic.diagnosis.title: Diagnostic criteria and clinical risk stratification
skill.ectopic.diagnosis.oneLine: Categorising stable unruptured versus ruptured ectopic pregnancy for management
skill.ectopic.diagnosis.why: Treatment selection hinges on objective criteria: haemodynamic stability, presence of cardiac activity, adnexal mass size, baseline beta-hCG, and reliable patient follow-up.

teach.heading: Establishing definitive diagnosis
teach.body:
Diagnosis is established when an extrauterine gestation is visualised on transvaginal ultrasound, or when serum beta-hCG exceeds the discriminatory zone with an empty uterine cavity and compatible adnexal findings.

In ambiguous cases where ultrasound remains inconclusive and the patient is stable, serial forty-eight hour beta-hCG monitoring and clinical reassessment identify the trend.

Diagnostic laparoscopy is indicated when imaging is non-diagnostic but clinical suspicion remains elevated or when acute symptoms develop during surveillance.

Uterine curettage to check for chorionic villi may be considered only after confirming that the pregnancy is non-viable and an intrauterine gestation has been excluded.

probes.q: What clinical criteria must all be satisfied before choosing medical management with methotrexate?
probes.a: The patient must be haemodynamically stable without significant pain, have an unruptured adnexal mass below thirty-five millimetres, no fetal cardiac activity, serum beta-hCG below fifteen hundred international units, and be able to attend follow-up.

probes.q: Under what clinical circumstances is surgical management preferred as first-line therapy?
probes.a: Surgery is first-line when there is haemodynamic instability, severe pain, adnexal mass thirty-five millimetres or larger, visible embryonic heartbeat, serum beta-hCG five thousand international units or higher, or inability to attend follow-up.

skill.tx.ectopic.title: Medical, surgical and emergency management of ectopic pregnancy
skill.tx.ectopic.oneLine: Methotrexate protocol, laparoscopic salpingectomy, and resuscitation in rupture
skill.tx.ectopic.why: Management must be tailored to clinical stability and fertility desires: medical management avoids surgical risks in compliant patients with small masses, while ruptured ectopic demands immediate resuscitation and operative haemostasis.
skill.tx.ectopic.dosingNote: This module teaches management at the level of drug class and principle, quoting only the single-dose methotrexate and anti-D regimens from the cited guidelines. All agents, doses, routes and monitoring schedules must be verified against current national and hospital protocols before administration. CliniX does not prescribe.

teach.heading: Medical management: the single-dose methotrexate protocol
teach.body:
Methotrexate is a folic acid antagonist that halts trophoblast proliferation by inhibiting dihydrofolate reductase during the synthesis phase of the cell cycle.

In suitable stable patients, the standard single-dose regimen is methotrexate 50 mg/m2 body surface area administered intramuscularly on day one.

Baseline complete blood count, renal function, liver enzymes, and blood group must be confirmed normal before administration.

Serum beta-hCG is measured on day four and day seven. A transient rise in hCG between day one and day four is common due to trophoblastic lysis.

If the beta-hCG falls by fifteen percent or more between day four and day seven, treatment is successful, and weekly hCG measurements continue until negative (under 5 IU/L).

If the fall is less than fifteen percent, a second dose of methotrexate 50 mg/m2 or surgical intervention is indicated.

Patients must avoid folic acid, non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, alcohol, and sexual intercourse, and report immediate pain.

teach.heading: Surgical management and emergency resuscitation in rupture
teach.body:
In ruptured ectopic pregnancy or haemodynamic collapse, resuscitation and theatre transfer proceed concurrently.

Immediate actions include two large-bore intravenous cannulae, rapid crystalloid infusion, crossmatching blood, and initiating the massive transfusion protocol if shock is profound.

Definitive surgery in unstable patients is emergency laparotomy or laparoscopy with total salpingectomy. Clamps are applied along the mesosalpinx from the fimbriated end to the cornua, coagulating or ligating the cornual junction.

In stable women desiring future fertility whose contralateral tube is diseased or absent, salpingotomy is considered: a 1 to 2 cm longitudinal incision is made over the antimesenteric border of the tube, products are evacuated, and haemostasis is secured.

Salpingotomy carries a three to twenty percent risk of persistent trophoblast, requiring weekly beta-hCG follow-up.

All non-sensitised Rh-negative women must receive anti-D immunoglobulin (250 IU before 20 weeks) within seventy-two hours.

probes.q: What percentage fall in serum beta-hCG between day four and day seven indicates successful medical management with methotrexate?
probes.a: A fall of fifteen percent or greater between day four and day seven indicates successful response to methotrexate.

probes.q: When is salpingotomy chosen over salpingectomy, and what key postoperative complication must be monitored?
probes.a: Salpingotomy is chosen when the patient wishes to preserve fertility and the contralateral tube is damaged or absent; the patient must be monitored with serial beta-hCG for persistent trophoblast.

probes.q: What instructions must be given to a woman receiving outpatient methotrexate regarding diet and medications?
probes.a: She must strictly avoid folic acid supplements which counteract the drug, avoid non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs which can worsen bleeding and mask pain, and abstain from alcohol and sexual intercourse.

probes.q: Why is a rise in serum beta-hCG between day one and day four after methotrexate not considered treatment failure?
probes.a: A transient rise between day one and day four is expected due to the release of hCG from lysed trophoblastic cells, which is why response is evaluated between day four and day seven.

probes.q: What threshold of serum beta-hCG defines complete biochemical resolution of ectopic pregnancy?
probes.a: Complete resolution is defined when serum beta-hCG drops to non-pregnant levels below five international units per litre.

skill.gen.appearance.finding: Alert, slightly pale young woman in mild to moderate abdominal discomfort, lying with hips slightly flexed; no jaundice, cyanosis, or peripheral oedema.

skill.gen.vitals.finding: Pulse 96 beats per minute, regular, normal volume; blood pressure 112/74 mmHg supine, 108/70 mmHg sitting; respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute; temperature 37.0 C; room air oxygen saturation 99%.

skill.exam.obg.gynae_abdominal.finding: Abdomen soft, not distended; marked localised tenderness on deep palpation in the right iliac fossa with mild voluntary guarding; no rebound tenderness; no generalised rigidity; bowel sounds audible and normal.

skill.exam.obg.vulval_inspect.finding: Normal external female genitalia; small amount of dark brownish blood trickling from the introitus; no active bright red haemorrhage.

skill.exam.obg.speculum_inspect.finding: Cervix appears normal, external os closed, dark brownish blood in the posterior fornix with no active arterial bleeding, no products of conception protruding through the cervical os.

skill.exam.obg.bimanual.finding: Exquisite cervical motion tenderness (excitation positive) on moving the cervix; uterus normal to slightly enlarged (~6 weeks size), soft, anteverted; tender, ill-defined boggy mass palpable in the right adnexa measuring approximately 3 cm, separate from the ovary; left adnexa non-tender; pouch of Douglas mildly tender without bulging.

skill.ectopic.signs.finding: Classic presentation of unruptured tubal ectopic pregnancy: amenorrhoea of 6 weeks, right iliac fossa tenderness with cervical motion tenderness, and dark vaginal spotting without frank peritonism or shock.

urine_hcg.label: Urine pregnancy test
urine_hcg.note: Confirms presence of urinary hCG at >=25 mIU/mL.

serum_beta_hcg.label: Serum quantitative beta-hCG
serum_beta_hcg.note: Baseline level below the transvaginal ultrasound discriminatory zone (1,500 mIU/mL); requires 48-hour repeat to assess trajectory if imaging is non-definitive.

transvaginal_usg.label: Transvaginal pelvic ultrasonography (TVS)
transvaginal_usg.result: Empty endometrial cavity with thickened decidual reaction (endometrial thickness 11 mm) and no intrauterine gestational sac. Well-defined hyperechoic tubal ring (bagel sign) in the right adnexa measuring 28 mm x 22 mm, separate from the right ovary, containing a small gestational sac with yolk sac but no visible embryo or cardiac activity. Left ovary and tube normal. Small amount of free fluid (depth 12 mm) in the pouch of Douglas.
transvaginal_usg.note: Confirms right unruptured tubal ectopic pregnancy below 35 mm without cardiac activity.

cbc_hb.label: Complete blood count
cbc_hb.result: Haemoglobin 11.8 g/dL, haematocrit 35.2%, total leukocyte count 7,800/mcL, platelets 245,000/mcL
cbc_hb.note: Baseline haematology normal; no acute anaemia or severe leukocytosis.

blood_group_rh.label: Blood group and Rh typing
blood_group_rh.note: Rh-negative status mandates anti-D immunoglobulin (250 IU) administration within 72 hours.

lft_rft.label: Liver and renal function tests
lft_rft.result: Serum creatinine 0.7 mg/dL, blood urea 22 mg/dL; AST 24 U/L, ALT 22 U/L, total bilirubin 0.6 mg/dL
lft_rft.note: Normal hepatic and renal function fulfills baseline safety criteria for methotrexate therapy.

differentialModel.answer: Right unruptured tubal ectopic pregnancy at 6 weeks gestation. Differential diagnoses include threatened or incomplete miscarriage, ruptured corpus luteum cyst, acute pelvic inflammatory disease, ovarian torsion, and acute appendicitis.

diagnosis.answer: Right unruptured tubal ectopic pregnancy at 6 weeks gestation in a B Rh-negative woman.

managementModel.answer: Admit for observation and evaluation. Administer single-dose intramuscular methotrexate 50 mg/m2 after confirming normal baseline hepatic and renal parameters. Administer anti-D immunoglobulin 250 IU for Rh-negative status within 72 hours. Measure repeat serum beta-hCG on day 4 and day 7. Counsel on warning symptoms of tubal rupture, avoiding NSAIDs, pelvic rest, and surgical escalation to laparoscopic salpingectomy if pain worsens or hCG fails to drop by 15% between day 4 and day 7.

teachingPoints: Assume any woman of reproductive age presenting with abdominal pain, amenorrhoea and abnormal vaginal bleeding has an ectopic pregnancy until proven otherwise.

Transvaginal ultrasound combined with serial quantitative serum beta-hCG is the diagnostic cornerstone; an empty uterine cavity above the discriminatory zone (1,500 to 2,000 mIU/mL) strongly indicates ectopic pregnancy.

Single-dose intramuscular methotrexate (50 mg/m2) is first-line for suitable stable unruptured ectopic pregnancies with hCG under 1,500 IU/L, mass size under 35 mm, absent embryonic cardiac activity, and guaranteed patient compliance.
All non-sensitised Rh-negative women with ectopic pregnancy must receive anti-D immunoglobulin prophylaxis within 72 hours.
